citation: Martin Monperrus (KTH Royal Institute of Technology), 'The End of Code Review: Coding Agents Supersede Human Inspection', arXiv:2606.13175v1 [cs.SE], 11 Jun 2026. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.13175 (PDF: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2606.13175)
source_tier: Preprint (arXiv, not peer reviewed). Position paper, about six pages.
access_status: Fully read (PDF opened and text extracted, all sections and references).
sponsor_and_incentive: No funding or acknowledgements statement found in the text. Author is an academic (KTH). No vendor sales interest evident. [uncertain] whether the arXiv abstract page lists anything more.
exact_quotes: "We do not present a new empirical study; instead, we synthesise existing capability evidence, and enumerate the implications for software engineering practice, tooling, and research." (Section I, Introduction)
"coding agents have reached a capability threshold at which human code review is redundant and should be replaced by agent-driven verification." (Section I)

"Our argument rests on two claims: every stated goal of code review can be served by agents at lower cost and higher throughput; the naive integration in which agents write code and humans remain the mandatory reviewers is a dead end because it neither provides meaningful assurance nor scales with AI-assisted throughput." (Abstract)

"In practice, reviews of agent-generated code become rubber-stamps: the human approves because the code looks correct, because the tests pass, and because the cognitive cost of genuine scrutiny is prohibitive [14]." (Section IV.B)
"The crossover point, at which the marginal benefit of human review no longer justifies its marginal cost, has already been reached." (Section IV.C)

"Human approval is not eliminated; it is reserved for the decisions that genuinely require it: high-risk changes, novel architecture choices, and regulated code paths where a named human must bear legal accountability." (Section V.A)
"A human reviewer who is unsure about a change will typically say so; an LLM may silently produce an approval." (Section VI.A)
"When the same model family that generates code is also responsible for reviewing it, there is a risk that generative and review blind spots are correlated" (Section VI.B)

"This is an active area of security research with no fully solved defences [32], and it represents a qualitatively new attack surface that does not exist for human reviewers." (Section VI.C, prompt injection of reviewer agents)

"Code review will not disappear overnight. Its role will refocus to a layer of high-stakes human oversight: architecture decisions with long-lived consequences, security-critical paths in regulated systems, and changes whose correctness depends on requirements that no agent has been given access to." (Section VII)
date_and_recency: Posted 11 Jun 2026 (v1). No original data collection. Capability evidence cited runs to late 2025 (SWE-bench leaderboard 2025; arXiv 2512.09882).
key_claims: Three claims in the body (the abstract says two): (1) every stated goal of review (defect detection, style, knowledge transfer, team awareness) can be met by agents at lower cost and higher throughput; (2) agent-writes/human-reviews is a dead end: human review gives no genuine assurance of agent code (becomes rubber-stamping) and does not scale with AI-assisted throughput; (3) the cost-benefit of mandatory human review has already flipped. Proposed: an independent agent reviews agent code, with humans only when agents flag uncertainty or a risk threshold is crossed. Humans retained for high-risk, architectural, regulated paths. Paper itself is more hedged in conclusion than title: 'will not disappear overnight', role refocuses to high-stakes oversight.
headline_figures: Developers at large organisations spend 'between ten and fifteen percent of their working hours' reading and commenting on others' code (cites Sadowski et al. 2018, Google). Review latency 'routinely stretches over twenty-four hours' (cites Hilton et al. 2016). Fagan inspections 'up to three percent of total project effort'. SWE-bench: GPT-4 with retrieval ~1.7%, SWE-agent ~12.5%, SWE-bench Verified >50% by late 2024, 'more than 70%' on public leaderboard late 2025 (Section III.A). NOTE internal inconsistency: Introduction says state-of-the-art agents 'resolve more than eighty percent of tasks'. AlphaCode 'top 54%' of Codeforces participants. No new numbers produced by the paper.
sample_unit_and_population: None. No sample. Synthesis of prior work: Bacchelli and Bird (Microsoft), Sadowski et al. (Google), Czerwonka et al. (Microsoft), CodeReviewer, Pornprasit and Tantithamthavorn, SWE-bench, Pearce et al. (Copilot CWE).
observed_vs_stated: Neither. Argumentative synthesis. Cited sources are a mix of observed behaviour (SWE-bench, review studies) and survey. The central premise that human review of agent code becomes rubber-stamping is asserted, with a citation to Czerwonka et al. that predates agent-written code, so it is not observed in agent-authored context.
what_makes_trust_justified: Independent agent review in CI as a structured merge gate: test coverage thresholds, security scan results, style compliance, reasoning traces. Ensemble review by multiple independent agents, ideally different models, requiring consensus. Calibrated uncertainty and abstention. Cyber-specialised frontier reviewers for security sign-off. Auditable, re-runnable structured reports (JSON, SARIF). Human escalation for flagged-uncertain or high-risk changes.
what_it_costs: Paper claims agent review is cheaper and instantaneous. It does not quantify agent review cost, false-positive rate or the human time to handle escalations. Acknowledges loss of informal knowledge transfer and tacit culture (needs pair programming, mentorship) and a new attack surface (prompt injection).
failure_mode_class: Wrong code (subtle semantic errors in plausible agent code), false report/silent approval by LLM reviewer, correlated blind spots between generator and reviewer, security, prompt injection of reviewer agents, over-reliance (human rubber-stamping), accountability gap.
control_that_would_have_prevented: Not an incident paper. Controls proposed: independent multi-model ensemble review, abstention/calibration, specialised security reviewers, treating reviewer prompt injection as first-class threat model, human sign-off on regulated and high-risk paths.
limitations_stated: States it is not an empirical study. Section VI lists its own counter-arguments: hallucination and false negatives, correlated generator/reviewer blind spots, prompt injection ('no fully solved defences'), architectural coherence, ethical accountability, loss of tacit knowledge transfer. Mitigations given are proposals, not tested. Claims to be 'the first to argue for the complete displacement of mandatory human code review'.
counter_evidence: Paper's own evidence is thin for its strongest claim: review benchmarks (CodeReviewer, Pornprasit) show 'comparable on a significant fraction' of a test set, not equivalence on real merges. The 'rubber-stamp' claim leans on Czerwonka (2015, human-authored code). Intro (>80%) vs Section III (>70%) SWE-bench figures disagree, and resolving issues is not the same as reviewing. Czerwonka's own finding is that review's value is knowledge transfer and maintainability, which the paper concedes yet says agents replace. External commentary (secondary, not opened here): Blake Crosley argues the paper conflates the reviewer role with the review; a separate June 2026 paper (c-CRAB) reportedly finds review agents address only about 40% of real review tasks [uncertain, from search snippets only]. Its own point that same-model generator and reviewer share blind spots cuts against its thesis.
verification_status: Paper's text: checked, primary source opened in full. Paper's cited figures (10-15% time, SWE-bench percentages, Czerwonka conclusion, Pearce CWE rates): NOT checked against the cited primary sources [uncertain]. c-CRAB 40% and Crosley critique: search snippets only [uncertain].
usable_claim: A June 2026 arXiv position paper by Martin Monperrus argues that coding agents have made mandatory human code review redundant for routine changes and that human review of agent-written code tends to become a rubber stamp. It presents no new empirical data, and itself lists correlated generator/reviewer blind spots and reviewer prompt injection as unresolved risks, and keeps humans for high-risk and regulated changes.
do_not_use: Do not present it as an empirical study or as evidence that agent review works. Do not use its SWE-bench numbers (80% vs 70% inconsistent) or the 10-15% review time figure without checking Sadowski et al. Do not say it claims review ends entirely; the conclusion says it will refocus, not vanish overnight. Do not cite 'rubber-stamp' as an observed finding.
overlap_with_existing_essays: [uncertain] Not checked against the Verification Gap or Checking Isn't Catching essays in this task. It is a strong foil: it argues the same human-review-as-theatre premise from the opposite conclusion.
